name: GAMBIA
tagline: A tiny land on a big river

flag.title: The Gambia
flag.note: Red, blue & green with white borders

lead: Gambia is the smallest country on mainland Africa. It is a thin strip along the Gambia River. Senegal wraps around it on three sides. People fish, farm and travel on the river every day.
geo: Gambia looks like a long thin finger pointing east. The Gambia River runs through the middle, with floodplains, mangrove swamps and savanna on its banks.
The land is so flat that nowhere is higher than a five-storey building. In the rainy season the river swells and floods the fields. Farmers grow rice and millet there.
animals: Gambia has over 560 kinds of birds, like bright bee-eaters and kingfishers. Baboons roam Abuko Nature Reserve, and green monkeys leap through riverside trees.
Nile crocodiles and hippos live in the river. At Kachikally's sacred pool, visitors touch the crocodiles. Locals call this a blessing.
culture: The kora has 21 strings and a body made from a giant gourd. Griots, who are singing storytellers, travel between villages. They keep old stories alive without writing them down.
Groundnuts (peanuts) appear in stews, sauces and snacks. The main meal is benachin, rice cooked with tomato and fish. Everyone eats from one shared bowl.
history: The Gambia River valley was part of the Mali Empire, which controlled the gold and salt trade. Portuguese sailors arrived in 1455. Britain later used Banjul to help end the slave trade.
Gambia gained independence on 18 February 1965. In the 1980s it joined Senegal as Senegambia, but the union ended in 1989. A long dictatorship ended in 2017.
wows: At its narrowest, Gambia is only about 24 km wide.
The Kachikally pool holds over 80 wild Nile crocodiles.
Over 560 bird species live in an area smaller than Yorkshire.
Kunta Kinteh Island, a former slave-trade fort, is a UNESCO site.
A kora can sound like a harp, a guitar and a drum at once.
From 1982 to 1989, Gambia and Senegal formed Senegambia.
The Gambia River runs over 1,100 km from Guinea to the sea.

myths.fact: Hippos can sprint about 30 km/h on land. That is faster than most people can run. They are among Africa's most dangerous animals.
Peanuts grow underground. After the flower dies, its stem bends down and pushes the pod into the soil.
